text: A long time ago, there was an Emperor who loved new clothes more than anything.
He spent all his money buying clothes and didn't care about his kingdom.
He had a new outfit for every hour of the day!
The Emperor was so focused on clothes that he didn't take time for his responsibilities, like ruling his kingdom.
It's important to balance fun things with things we need to do, like schoolwork or helping others.
One day, two people came to town and said they made special clothes.
If someone was smart and very good at their job, they would be able to see the clothes,
but if they were lazy and unfit for their job, the clothes would be invisible!
The Emperor had never heard of such a thing before!
The two clothesmakers told the Emperor he should buy an outfit from them for a big bag of gold.

The Emperor should take a moment to think about whether the clothes were real or not.
The Emperor should say no because doing your job is not important.

text: Saying yes immediately does not give the Emperor time to decide whether the clothesmakers' claim is real.
He should think carefully first.

text: Unfortunately, the Emperor did not think about whether the clothes were real or not.
He paid the clothesmakers to make the clothes right away.
As soon as the Emperor left the room, the clothesmakers began to laugh.
"What a fool! There is no such thing as invisible clothes! Now we are rich!" one of them said.
The next day, the two clothesmakers pretended to weave on empty looms and asked for more money for special silk and thread.
They worked all day, but there was no fabric at all.
When the Emperor was not around, they would nap and eat snacks instead.
The Emperor sent his old, wise minister to check on the clothes that night.
"Tell me what they look like," the Emperor ordered.
When the minister arrived at the clothesmakers' room, he did not see anything on the looms.
One of the clothesmakers said to the minister, "Oh, if you are the Emperor's minister, you must be very good at your job!
You should be able to see the clothes.
Aren't the patterns beautiful?"
The minister didn't reply.
He returned to the Emperor's room afterward, and the Emperor asked how they looked.

The old, wise minister should say he forgot to check since he does not want to tell the Emperor the truth.
The old, wise minister should be honest because being honest helps us avoid mistakes later.

text: Lying would hide the problem and could allow the Emperor to make more mistakes.

text: Being honest helps people recognize problems and avoid mistakes later.
The old, wise minister unfortunately was not honest and lied.
He said, "Oh, it's beautiful!"
The Emperor sent more people to check, and they all said the same thing:
"Oh, it's beautiful!" even though there was nothing there.
Finally, the clothesmakers came to the Emperor and told him they had finished the outfit.
They pulled a hanger out of a bag, with nothing on it.
The Emperor also did not want to look foolish, so he pretended to see the clothes too.
He said, "How magnificent!" even though he knew he couldn't see anything.
The people pretended to dress the Emperor in the invisible clothes.
They said the clothes were so light that he could hardly feel them, and they told him they could make him even more outfits!
They said a great ruler should only be wearing the finest of clothing.

choices.text: The Emperor should admit his mistake and wear other clothes.

text: Admitting his mistake would let the Emperor tell the truth and make a better choice.

text: As the Emperor paraded through the streets, everyone cheered and said, "How beautiful!"
But a little child looked up and said, "He hasn't got anything on!"
Everyone laughed and realized the truth.
The Emperor was embarrassed but kept walking, because he didn't want to admit his mistake.
The little child had the courage to speak the truth.
Sometimes, even when everyone else is quiet, it's important to say what's right.
Telling the truth is important, but so is making sure our friends' feelings are not hurt.
Pretend someone you know accidentally does something wrong, like putting their shoes on the wrong feet:
how could you tell them the truth without making them feel bad?
